verses.translation_literal: Song of the ascents. Behold, bless YHWH, all [you] servants of YHWH, those standing in the house of YHWH in the nights.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the going up. Come, then. Bless the LORD, all you who serve the LORD, you who stand in the house of the LORD while the nights go by.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the last of the fifteen Songs of the Ascents, the pilgrim collection (Psalms 120–134), and it ends with the pilgrims at the gate and the lamps still lit. The opening 'Behold' (hinneh) is a hand on the shoulder: look, now, the time has come. Do not play it as a lecture. Play it as a call across a dark courtyard.

Who are 'the servants who stand'? The Hebrew verb 'omdim is the technical word for those on duty: priests and Levites 'stand' to minister. The commentators differ on who exactly: Ibn Ezra takes the poet to be speaking to the priests, Radak to the devout who rise from their beds at night to pray, and the Targum has them 'guarding' the sanctuary. The 'nights' are plural and meant literally, since the Temple was never wholly quiet: the night watches kept the fires, guarded the gates and sang. An actor can use that: these people are tired, and the call to bless is also a call to stay awake.

The KJV 'by night' and 'which ... stand' is accurate in sense but turns the plural 'nights' into one night and smooths over the participle 'those who stand' into a relative clause. The KJV also prints 'A Song of degrees' as a separate heading (134:0 in its numbering), though in the Hebrew it is part of verse 1; 'degrees' is the old rendering of ma'alot, 'steps' or 'ascents', whether of the Temple stairs, of the pilgrims going up to Jerusalem, or of the poem's own stepped refrains. YHWH appears three times in one line, a drumbeat that makes the whole verse a naming of the Name.

One sound detail: 'bless' (barakh) opens a root the poem repeats in every verse, so the whole psalm is a loop of blessing from people to God, and from God back to people.

philological_notes.note: A presentative particle, 'look!' or 'now!'. It draws the hearers' attention and marks a turn in the action; here it opens the call. The KJV 'Behold' keeps it, the BBE drops it.

The root brk means to bless. When humans bless God the sense is praise, to speak well of him and acknowledge him as the source of good. When God blesses people it is gift and favour. The psalm turns on this one root: the first two verses are people blessing God, the last is God blessing them.
'Those who stand', a participle with the article. Standing is the posture of service before a superior; priests and Levites 'stand' to minister, as in Deut 10:8 and 2 Chr 29:11.

verses.translation_literal: Lift up your hands [in] holiness, and bless YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lift your hands, open and empty, toward the holy place, and bless the LORD.
verses.directors_commentary:
The command is physical: hands raised, palms open and turned up. In the ancient Near East this is the posture of prayer and of surrender, shown in reliefs and described in the Psalms (28:2, 141:2). Blessing here is something the body does as well as the mouth. The actors should move before they speak.

The Hebrew word qodesh stands bare, with no preposition, and that ambiguity is real. It can mean 'in the sanctuary' (KJV, YLT), 'toward the sanctuary' (ASV), or 'in holiness', as Meiri takes it ('in sanctity, in purity, with perfect intention'). The KJV chooses 'in the sanctuary' and so fixes the place and loses the other readings. The literal layer therefore keeps the word bare. Radak reads the verse as the priestly gesture of blessing the people, but prefers the plain prayer posture, and says qodesh may mean 'toward the holy place'.

Note that the Hebrew 'lift up' (se'u) and 'bless' (barakhu) are both plural imperatives: it is a chorus, not a solo. The BBE rearranges the verse into a single act, 'give praise ... lifting up your hands', which loses the two-step rhythm: first lift, then bless.

philological_notes.note: 'Lift up your hands'. The same verb nasa' is used of lifting the eyes, the voice or the face. Lifting the hands is the gesture of prayer and also of priestly blessing (Lev 9:22, where Aaron lifts his hands toward the people).
'Holiness' or 'holy place'. With no preposition it can be an accusative of place or manner: 'in/toward the sanctuary' or 'in holiness'. Both are possible, and the commentators take both.

verses.translation_literal: May YHWH bless you from Zion, maker of heaven and earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And may the LORD bless you from Zion, he who made the heavens and the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice changes. Verses 1–2 were plural commands; this is a single blessing, and 'you' is singular. Someone answers the night-watchers, perhaps the priests speaking to the pilgrims or the departing worshipper, perhaps the poet to each listener in turn. Radak says it is the poet's own voice (if you bless him, he will bless you); Meiri hears it as something said to the people, or to the king. Whoever speaks, the last line should be the quietest of the psalm: the long night ends in a blessing sent back.

The KJV, 'The Lord that made heaven and earth bless thee out of Zion', moves the words about the maker to the front, so that the sentence starts with the Creator; the Hebrew puts the verb first, 'may he bless you', and the title last, as a closing weight. Metzudat David notes that the clause is displaced and that 'maker of heaven and earth' belongs with 'YHWH'. The YLT and ASV keep the Hebrew order, and the BBE follows the KJV: is it 'may he bless you ... the maker' or 'may the maker bless you'? The KJV also archaizes with 'thee' and 'out of', where the Hebrew has a plain 'from' (min).

Why end on this title? The Hebrew leaves the logic of the line to the hearer, and the commentators draw it out in different ways. Radak hears in 'maker of heaven and earth' the heavens that give the blessing of rain and the earth that yields its produce, all at his command. Malbim reads it the other way: the blessing does not come through the ordinary order of the heavens but from Zion, from the one who made both. In a farming world a blessing means rain, grain and children, and either way the line says it has one source and one place. The preposition min ('from') matters: Zion is where the Presence dwells, and the blessing travels outward from it to the home village.

philological_notes.note: A wish: 'may he bless you'. The suffix is 2nd masculine singular, in contrast to the plural address of the previous verses. It has the same verb form and subject as the opening of the priestly blessing in Num 6:24, 'YHWH bless you and keep you'.
'From Zion': the blessing has a point of origin, the place of the divine presence. Radak and Metzudat David both say the blessing issues from Zion because the Presence dwells there.

'Maker of heaven and earth', a stock title for the creator. 'Heaven' is a plural-form noun (shamayim) with no singular. The same title recurs in the Ascents at Psalms 121:2 and 124:8, so the collection closes on a phrase it has used before.
